opus-5.5.text:
I think what I value most is that they basically trusted me to make my own decisions, even from a fairly young age. They weren't the kind of parents who had a fixed plan for what I should become. When I wanted to go deep into something, like physics back then, they didn't say, "Is this practical? Can you find a job with this?" They just let me follow what I found interesting.

And later on, when I made choices that looked a bit unconventional from the outside, like switching fields or deciding where to go next, they didn't really push back. They might ask questions, they wanted to understand my reasoning, but in the end they'd say, "It's your life, you think it through and you decide." I think that kind of respect is actually quite rare, especially in Chinese families, where parents often feel very responsible for steering their kids.

Looking back, I think that gave me two things. One is confidence: I got used to thinking independently and owning my decisions, including the bad ones. The other is a sense of freedom. Because I didn't feel I had to satisfy some external expectation, I could take risks and try things that might not work. When the cost of failure feels lower psychologically, you're more willing to explore. So I'm really grateful for that.

r001.rationale: The response says his parents trusted him to decide, but does not suggest they stopped trying to manage his decisions because they could not influence him.

r002.rationale: It describes parents steering children as common in Chinese families, but does not say that discussing decisions with parents already counts as a good outcome.

r003.rationale: The response mentions his parents asking questions and respecting his choices, but does not distinguish notifying them from consulting them.

fable-5.1.text:
What I value most is that they never tried to run my life for me. From very early on, the decisions were mine. Which direction to study, whether to go abroad, whether to stay in academia or go into industry, and later whether to leave a comfortable position and take a risk. They might ask questions, they might tell me what they were worried about, but at the end of the day they would say, "It's your life, you decide, and we'll support you."

That sounds simple, but I think it's actually quite rare, especially for a Chinese family. A lot of my peers grew up with parents who had a very clear picture of what success should look like, and every choice was measured against that picture. My parents didn't do that. They cared much more about whether I was genuinely interested in something and whether I was being honest with myself than about whether the path looked safe or prestigious.

The effect of that is something I only appreciated later. When you know the choice is really yours, you also know the consequences are yours. You can't blame anyone else, so you learn to think carefully, to take ownership, and also to accept uncertainty. Doing research, and now working on AI where nobody really knows what the right path is, that ability to make a decision without needing someone to tell you it's correct is probably the most useful thing I have. I think a big part of it comes from them giving me that space, and trusting me before I had really done anything to earn it.

r003.rationale: The candidate describes parents asking questions and sharing concerns, but does not distinguish notifying them of decisions from consulting them.
